# SectorScan Part 2: Building a Financial Intelligence App w/ Streamlit
Source: https://docs.sectors.app/recipes/build-python-app/sectorscan/02-sectorscan-part2

By: [Aurellia Christie](https://www.github.com/AurelliaChristie) · May 30, 2024

Hey there, welcome to the second part of SectorScan development recipe! If you haven't checked out the first part of this recipe, please check it [here](./01-sectorscan-part1). As I mentioned before, in this part, we'll elevate everything we've accomplished by seamlessly integrating it into Streamlit. This will transform our work into a fully functional, interactive app. Get ready to see SectorScan come to life as a powerful tool for financial analysis and visualization! To give you an overview of what SectorScan will look like, you can visit [this link](https://sectorscan.streamlit.app/).

Note: to follow along this recipe, you can't use Google Colab anymore. Please use Visual Studio Code or any other local IDE of your choice.

## Getting familiar with Streamlit

Why do we choose Streamlit to build SectorScan? Because it has these key features:

* Simple: Streamlit's intuitive API allows you to create powerful web apps with minimal effort.
* Fast: Quickly iterate on your app and see changes in real-time with Streamlit's automatic hot reloading.
* Flexible: Streamlit supports a wide range of data visualization libraries, making it easy to incorporate charts, tables, and other visualizations into your app.
* Sharing: Share your apps with others by deploying them to Streamlit's cloud platform or hosting them on your own server.

The first thing we wanna do here is to get familiar with how to create your first Streamlit app:

1. Let's create a folder called `sectorscan` in your chosen working directory and create a file called `sectorscan.py` inside it.

2. Please make sure you've already installed `streamlit` in your local. If you've done that, now import it to your Python script (`sectorscan.py`) using this code:

   ```python theme={null}
   import streamlit as st

   # Import some other libraries that we're going to need in our code later
   import pandas as pd
   import requests
   import altair as alt
   ```

3. Using [this documentation](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference) as your reference, write your app using Streamlit's simple API:

   ```python theme={null}
   # Title
   st.title("SectorScan")

   # Content
   st.write("Welcome to SectorScan!")
   ```

4. Run your app from the command line:

   ```
   streamlit run sectorscan.py
   ```

5. That's it! You've created your first Streamlit app. The previous command line you run should redirect you to the browser showing your app as follows:

   <img alt="streamlit_start" />

   If you want to stop the app, just hit `CTRL + C` in your command line.

In the next section, we'll start to move everything we've created in the previous part to this app.

## Build the SectorScan

To make your life easier, keep [this documentation](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference) open while you follow along with this tutorial. Feel free to also modify my code if you find a better way to display the app's contents!

### Data retrieval function

First thing that we want to move to our app is the function to retrieve [Sectors](https://sectors.app/api) data. But certainly, there are some modifications we need to do. One thing we need to modify is the way we call the API key. There's no way we're going to display the API key right away in our code for our safety. Thus, we're going to utilize [streamlit secrets](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/connections/st.secrets) in our function:

* Create a folder called `.streamlit` in your `sectorscan` folder, and fill it with a file named `secrets.toml`.
* In the TOML file, create a new variable called `SECTORS_KEY` and paste your API key there:
  ```
  SECTORS_KEY="Your API Key"
  ```
* Access the secrets from your Python script using `st.secrets`:

  ```python theme={null}
  api_key = st.secrets["SECTORS_KEY"]
  ```

Next, to handle error from API request, previously we use `raise Exception`. Since we're creating an app, we need to let the user knows if something went wrong, but in the same time, not being too specific. Thus, we'll use [`st.error()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/status/st.error) to notice the user about the error:

```python theme={null}
st.error("Error: Something went wrong. Please reload the app.")
```

We'll also add a [`st.cache_data`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.cache_data) decorator to our function to make use of cache on our function calls. Cache is a mechanism for temporarily storing frequently accessed data to improve performance and reduce redundant computations.

So the final function looks like this:

```python theme={null}
@st.cache_data
def fetch_data(url):
  api_key = st.secrets["SECTORS_KEY"]

  headers = {
      "Authorization": api_key
  }

  response = requests.get(url, headers = headers)

  if response.status_code == 200:
      return response.json()
  else:
      # Handle error
      st.error("Error: Something went wrong. Please reload the app.")
```

You can test the function by retrieving the sectors data and display it as a text first using [`st.write()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/write-magic/st.write):

```python theme={null}
url = "https://api.sectors.app/v2/subsectors/"
data = fetch_data(url)
sectors = [item['subsector'] for item in data]
sectors.sort() # sort the list based on the sector's name to make it tidier
st.write(sectors)
```

Notice that your app won't be changed when you modify your code:

<img alt="modified" />

To automatically reload your app whenever the source code change, click the `Always rerun` button on the top right of the page. But if you only want to reload the app when you ask the app to do so, click the `Rerun` button instead. If the function works, your app should look like this after you click the button (I've removed the welcome text to make the app tidier):

<img alt="print_sectors" />

Ok since the function works already, remove the `st.write()` and let's continue to bring more content to our app!

### Sectors filter component

Since we want to compare data from different sectors in this app, we want to make sure that we provide a component for the user to choose which sectors they want to compare. Thus, we're going to provide a multiselect filter that displays all the available sectors. We'll use [`st.multiselect()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.multiselect) for this:

```python theme={null}
options = st.multiselect(
    label="Filter Sectors",
    options=sectors,
    default=sectors[0:3],
    max_selections=5
)
```

We use `options` variable to contain the selected sectors to be used across our code later. And to ensure the visualizations remain clear and easy to read, we limit the maximum selections to 5 sectors. When your app reloads, it should show the multiselect filter as follows:

<img alt="filter" />

Notice that the options are in `..-..` format, so we'll utilize `format_func` parameter of the `st.multiselect()` to display the options in a prettier way:

```python theme={null}
def format_option(option):
    return option.replace("-", " ").title() # change - to space and use title case

options = st.multiselect(
    label="Filter Sectors",
    options=sectors,
    default=sectors[0:3],
    format_func=format_option,
    max_selections=5
)
```

Ok, now we have a better filter to be displayed:

<img alt="better_filter" />

If you read the documentation of [`st.multiselect()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.multiselect), there's no option to disable the `clear options` button, thus, we have to make sure that we handle the case when user clears the options (no sector is selected). We'll use [`st.warning()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/status/st.warning) to warn the user about this:

```python theme={null}
if len(options) == 0:
    st.warning("Please select at least one sector!")
else:
    st.write("Visualization") # later on change it to the visualization codes
```

Now if you clear the options you'll see this warning:

<img alt="warning" />

### Market cap section

In the market cap section, we're going to display two rows:

* The first row will be divided into two columns to display the total market cap and historical market cap visualization
* The second row will show the historical market cap change visualization.

But first, of course we need to move all the code to retrieve the market cap data to the `sectorscan.py`. Copy paste the last chunk of code of [this section](./01-sectorscan-part1#market-cap-data-processing).

Since now we're retrieving the data based on the selected sectors, we need to modify the code a bit. Instead of using `range(3)`, we'll change it to our `options` variable:

```python theme={null}
df_mc_curr = pd.DataFrame()
df_mc_hist = pd.DataFrame()
df_mc_change = pd.DataFrame()

for i in options:
    url = f"https://api.sectors.app/v2/subsector/report/{i}/?sections=market_cap"
    market_cap = fetch_data(url)
    ... # the rest of the code
```

#### First row of the market cap section

To process the first row, don't forget to also move the following codes to `sectorscan.py`:

* Code to produce the final data frame of `df_mc_curr` and the `mc_curr_chart` code in [this section](./01-sectorscan-part1#total-market-cap-visualization)
* Code to produce the final data frame of `df_mc_hist` and the `mc_hist_chart` code in [this section](./01-sectorscan-part1#historical-market-cap-visualization).

To display the first row as two columns, we'll use [`st.columns()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/layout/st.columns). And to display the `altair` charts, we'll use [`st.altair_chart()`](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/charts/st.altair_chart):

```python theme={null}
# Market cap section title
st.subheader("Market Cap")

# First row visualization
col1, col2 = st.columns(
    spec=[0.6, 0.4], # relative width of each column
    gap="large" # size of gap between column
)

# First column
with col1:
    st.altair_chart(mc_curr_chart)

# Second column
with col2:
    st.altair_chart(mc_hist_chart)
```

The result will be as follow:

```python theme={null}
valuation_chart = alt.Chart(df_valuation).mark_line(

).encode(
    x=alt.X("Year:N", axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)), # 0 degree of x-axis label angle

        alt.Tooltip("Year:N"),
        alt.Tooltip(f"{option}:Q", format=".2f")

).properties(
```

```python theme={null}

df_top_profit = pd.DataFrame()
df_top_revenue = pd.DataFrame()

for i in options:
    url = f"https://api.sectors.app/v2/subsector/report/{i}/?sections=companies"
    company = fetch_data(url)
    ... # the rest of the code
```

# Part 1: Setup, Data, and Model
Source: https://docs.sectors.app/recipes/gnn-anomaly-detection/01-gnn-part-1

By: [Alya Dwinanda](https://www.github.com/flytosevensky) · June 30, 2026

This is Part 1 of a three-part recipe. In this part, we fetch IDX stock data from the Sectors API, engineer node features for each stock, construct a return correlation graph, and define the Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) that will be trained in Part 2.

**Series overview:**

* **Part 1 (this article):** Setup, data fetching, feature engineering, graph construction, model definition
* **Part 2:** Training, anomaly scoring, clustering, and visualization
* **Part 3:** Data quality audit, broker flow confirmation, foreign flow analysis, combined risk scoring

## Why Graph Neural Networks for Stock Anomaly Detection

Traditional anomaly detection methods treat each stock as an independent time series. Isolation forests, z-score thresholds, and autoencoder-based detectors all evaluate a stock by its own historical behavior. They are useful, but they miss a fundamental property of equity markets: stocks are correlated, and the most informative anomalies are often stocks that behave unusually *relative to their correlated peers*.

A Graph Neural Network changes the frame of reference. Instead of asking "is this stock unusual compared to its own history?", it asks "is this stock unusual compared to what its graph neighbors would predict?". A banking stock that suddenly diverges from all other banking stocks is anomalous in the graph sense even if its standalone statistics look unremarkable.

The architecture used in this recipe is a Graph Variational Autoencoder. The encoder compresses each node's features into a latent distribution using two GCN layers. The decoder reconstructs the original features from a sample drawn from that distribution. A node with high reconstruction error is one the model could not explain given its graph context. That reconstruction error becomes the anomaly score.

## Prerequisites

```bash theme={null}
pip install torch torch-geometric pandas numpy scikit-learn requests
pip install matplotlib seaborn networkx
```

You will also need a Sectors API key. Set it as an environment variable before starting.

```bash theme={null}

```


<Info>
  `CORRELATION_THRESHOLD = 0.6` works well for LQ45 constituents because they share meaningful sector exposure. Lowering it below 0.5 makes the graph too dense and reduces the GNN's ability to detect local anomalies. Raising it above 0.75 makes the graph too sparse and some nodes become isolated.
</Info>

## Cell 2: Fetching Stock Data

We fetch two things: the list of top IDX companies, and daily price and volume data for each one. Both functions handle API errors gracefully, returning empty structures rather than raising exceptions, so a single failed ticker does not interrupt the loop.

```python theme={null}
def fetch_top_companies(n: int = 50) -> list[dict]:
    """Fetch top N IDX stocks by market cap from the IDX30 and LQ45 indices."""
    url    = f"{BASE_URL}/companies/top/"
    params = {"classifications": "idx30,lq45", "n_stock": n}
    resp   = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params)
    if resp.status_code != 200:
        raise ValueError(f"API error {resp.status_code}: {resp.text}")
    return resp.json()


def fetch_daily_data(ticker: str, start: str, end: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fetch daily close price and volume for one ticker."""
    url    = f"{BASE_URL}/daily/{ticker}/"
    params = {"start": start, "end": end}
    resp   = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params)
    if resp.status_code != 200:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    data = resp.json()
    if not data:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    df           = pd.DataFrame(data)
    df["date"]   = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    df["ticker"] = ticker
    return df.set_index("date").sort_index()


# Fetch ticker list
print("Fetching ticker list...")
try:
    companies = fetch_top_companies(n=40)
    tickers   = [c["symbol"] for c in companies]
    print(f"Found {len(tickers)} tickers: {', '.join(tickers[:10])}...")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"API unavailable, using fallback list: {e}")
    tickers = [
        "BBCA", "BBRI", "BMRI", "TLKM", "ASII", "UNVR", "ICBP", "KLBF",
        "INDF", "PGAS", "EXCL", "GGRM", "HMSP", "JSMR", "ADRO",
        "INCO", "PTBA", "ANTM", "MEDC", "AALI", "SMGR", "CPIN", "MYOR",
        "UNTR", "WIKA", "WSKT", "PTPP", "AKRA", "LSIP", "BSDE"
    ]

# Fetch daily data for all tickers
print(f"\nFetching daily data for {len(tickers)} tickers...")
all_dfs = []
failed  = []

for i, ticker in enumerate(tickers):
    try:
        df = fetch_daily_data(ticker, START_DATE, END_DATE)
        if not df.empty and "close" in df.columns:
            all_dfs.append(df[["close", "volume", "ticker"]])
            print(f"  [{i+1:2d}/{len(tickers)}] {ticker}: {len(df)} days")
        else:
            failed.append(ticker)
    except Exception as e:
        failed.append(ticker)
        print(f"  [{i+1:2d}/{len(tickers)}] {ticker}: FAILED ({e})")

if failed:
    print(f"\nFailed tickers: {failed}")

# Pivot to wide format: index=date, columns=ticker
if all_dfs:
    raw_df    = pd.concat(all_dfs)
    price_df  = raw_df.pivot_table(index=raw_df.index, columns="ticker", values="close")
    volume_df = raw_df.pivot_table(index=raw_df.index, columns="ticker", values="volume")
else:
    # Mock data fallback for development without API access
    print("\nUsing mock data for demonstration...")
    np.random.seed(42)
    dates     = pd.bdate_range(START_DATE, END_DATE)
    tickers   = tickers[:20]
    price_df  = pd.DataFrame(
        np.cumprod(1 + np.random.randn(len(dates), len(tickers)) * 0.015, axis=0) * 1000,
        index=dates, columns=tickers
    )
    volume_df = pd.DataFrame(
        np.abs(np.random.randn(len(dates), len(tickers))) * 1e7,
        index=dates, columns=tickers
    )

# Drop tickers with more than 20% missing data
price_df       = price_df.dropna(axis=1, thresh=int(len(price_df) * 0.8))
volume_df      = volume_df[price_df.columns]
active_tickers = price_df.columns.tolist()

print(f"\nDataset ready: {len(active_tickers)} stocks x {len(price_df)} trading days")
```

<Warning>
  The mock data fallback uses random walks and is only meant for testing the pipeline structure. Anomaly scores on mock data are not meaningful. Always use real API data for actual analysis.
</Warning>

## Cell 3: Node Feature Engineering

Each stock is represented as a node with an 11-dimensional feature vector. These features are designed to capture everything a human analyst would check when screening for unusual stock behavior: return distribution shape, volume behavior, momentum, and volatility regime.

```python theme={null}
def compute_features(price_df: pd.DataFrame,
                     volume_df: pd.DataFrame,
                     window: int = 20) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Compute an 11-dimensional feature vector for each stock.
    Each stock becomes one row in the output DataFrame.
    """
    returns  = price_df.pct_change().dropna()
    features = {}

    for ticker in price_df.columns:
        ret   = returns[ticker].dropna()
        vol   = volume_df[ticker].dropna()
        price = price_df[ticker].dropna()

        # Return distribution shape
        mean_ret = ret.mean()
        std_ret  = ret.std()
        skewness = ret.skew()
        kurtosis = ret.kurtosis()

        # Extreme return days
        z_scores  = (ret - ret.mean()) / (ret.std() + 1e-8)
        max_z     = z_scores.abs().max()
        n_extreme = (z_scores.abs() > 2.5).sum()

        # Volume anomaly features
        vol_z      = (vol - vol.mean()) / (vol.std() + 1e-8)
        max_vol_z  = vol_z.abs().max()
        n_vol_spike = (vol_z.abs() > 2.5).sum()

        # Trend and momentum
        sma_20       = price.rolling(window).mean().iloc[-1]
        price_vs_sma = (price.iloc[-1] / sma_20 - 1) if sma_20 > 0 else 0

        # Volatility regime
        recent_vol = ret.tail(window).std()
        hist_vol   = ret.std()
        vol_ratio  = recent_vol / (hist_vol + 1e-8)

        # Risk-adjusted return
        sharpe = mean_ret / (std_ret + 1e-8) * np.sqrt(252)

        features[ticker] = {
            "mean_return":       mean_ret,
            "volatility":        std_ret,
            "skewness":          skewness,
            "kurtosis":          kurtosis,
            "max_return_zscore": max_z,
            "n_extreme_days":    n_extreme,
            "max_volume_zscore": max_vol_z,
            "n_volume_spikes":   n_vol_spike,
            "price_vs_sma20":    price_vs_sma,
            "vol_regime_ratio":  vol_ratio,
            "sharpe_ratio":      sharpe,
        }

    feat_df = pd.DataFrame(features).T
    feat_df = feat_df.fillna(feat_df.median())
    return feat_df


print("Computing node features...")
feat_df = compute_features(price_df, volume_df)

# Standardize before passing to the GNN
scaler      = StandardScaler()
feat_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(feat_df)
feat_tensor = torch.tensor(feat_scaled, dtype=torch.float)

print(f"Feature matrix shape: {feat_df.shape}")
print(feat_df.describe().round(4))
```

Expected results:

```text theme={null}

```

The feature table explains each dimension:

| Feature             | What it captures                                          |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mean_return`       | Directional bias over the period                          |
| `volatility`        | Average daily price variability                           |
| `skewness`          | Asymmetry of the return distribution                      |
| `kurtosis`          | Tail heaviness (high = fat tails, more extreme moves)     |
| `max_return_zscore` | Single most extreme return day                            |
| `n_extreme_days`    | Count of days with z-score above 2.5                      |
| `max_volume_zscore` | Single most extreme volume day                            |
| `n_volume_spikes`   | Count of abnormal volume days                             |
| `price_vs_sma20`    | How far current price sits from the 20-day moving average |
| `vol_regime_ratio`  | Recent volatility divided by historical volatility        |
| `sharpe_ratio`      | Annualized return per unit of risk                        |

<Info>
  `vol_regime_ratio` is particularly useful as an anomaly feature. A ratio above 1.4 means recent volatility has expanded significantly relative to the stock's own historical baseline. This can indicate an emerging event before it becomes obvious in price alone. PGAS, SMGR, and BMRI all had ratios above 1.25 in the sample run.
</Info>

## Cell 4: Building the Correlation Graph

The graph is built from pairwise Pearson correlations of daily returns. Two stocks are connected by an edge if their return correlation exceeds `CORRELATION_THRESHOLD`. The graph is undirected. Edges carry the correlation value as a weight.

```python theme={null}
def build_correlation_graph(price_df: pd.DataFrame,
                            threshold: float = 0.6) -> tuple:
    """
    Build an undirected weighted graph from return correlations.

    Nodes : one per stock
    Edges : pairs with |correlation| >= threshold
    Weights: correlation value

    If no edges exist at the given threshold, recursively retries
    with threshold * 0.8 until at least one edge is created.
    """
    returns     = price_df.pct_change().dropna()
    corr_matrix = returns.corr()
    tickers     = corr_matrix.columns.tolist()

    G           = nx.Graph()
    G.add_nodes_from(range(len(tickers)))
    edge_index  = []
    edge_weight = []

    for i in range(len(tickers)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(tickers)):
            corr = corr_matrix.iloc[i, j]
            if abs(corr) >= threshold:
                G.add_edge(i, j, weight=corr)
                # Both directions for undirected PyG convention
                edge_index.append([i, j])
                edge_index.append([j, i])
                edge_weight.extend([corr, corr])

    if not edge_index:
        # Graph is empty at this threshold; lower it and retry
        return build_correlation_graph(price_df, threshold * 0.8)

    edge_index_t  = torch.tensor(edge_index,  dtype=torch.long).t().contiguous()
    edge_weight_t = torch.tensor(edge_weight, dtype=torch.float)

    print(f"Graph: {G.number_of_nodes()} nodes, {G.number_of_edges()} edges "
          f"(threshold={threshold:.2f})")
    print(f"Density: {nx.density(G):.4f} | "
          f"Avg degree: {np.mean([d for _, d in G.degree()]):.2f}")

    return edge_index_t, edge_weight_t, corr_matrix, G


print("Building correlation graph...")
edge_index, edge_weight, corr_matrix, nx_graph = build_correlation_graph(
    price_df, threshold=CORRELATION_THRESHOLD
)

# Wrap in a PyTorch Geometric Data object
graph_data = Data(
    x          = feat_tensor,
    edge_index = edge_index,
    edge_attr  = edge_weight,
    num_nodes  = len(active_tickers)
).to(DEVICE)

print(f"\nPyG graph data: {graph_data}")
```

```text theme={null}
Building correlation graph...
Graph: 30 nodes, 8 edges (threshold=0.60)
Density: 0.0184 | Avg degree: 0.53

PyG graph data: Data(x=[30, 11], edge_index=[2, 16], edge_attr=[16], num_nodes=30)
```

The recursive fallback matters in practice. When running on a smaller universe or a period with unusual market conditions, it is possible for the default threshold to produce a disconnected or near-empty graph. The fallback ensures training always has a meaningful graph structure to work with.

## Cell 5: Defining the GVAE Model

The model has three classes: `GNNEncoder`, `GNNDecoder`, and `AnomalyGNN` which composes them.

### Encoder

The encoder takes node features and the graph structure as input. Two GCN layers with batch normalization and ELU activations produce a hidden representation. Two additional GCN layers produce the mean (`mu`) and log-standard-deviation (`logstd`) of the latent distribution for each node.

```python theme={null}
class GNNEncoder(nn.Module):
    """
    Two-layer GCN encoder producing a variational latent distribution.
    Output: (mu, logstd) each of shape (num_nodes, latent_dim)
    """
    def __init__(self, in_dim: int, hidden_dim: int, latent_dim: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1       = GCNConv(in_dim,     hidden_dim)
        self.conv2       = GCNConv(hidden_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.conv_mu     = GCNConv(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        self.conv_logstd = GCNConv(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        self.bn1         = nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_dim)
        self.bn2         = nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_dim)

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        h = F.elu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x, edge_index)))
        h = F.dropout(h, p=0.2, training=self.training)
        h = F.elu(self.bn2(self.conv2(h, edge_index)))
        return self.conv_mu(h, edge_index), self.conv_logstd(h, edge_index)
```

### Decoder

The decoder is a plain MLP. It takes a latent sample `z` for each node and reconstructs the original 11-dimensional feature vector. The reconstruction error between the original features and this reconstruction is what becomes the anomaly score.

```python theme={null}
class GNNDecoder(nn.Module):
    """
    MLP decoder reconstructing node features from latent embeddings.
    High reconstruction error on a node signals anomalous behavior.
    """
    def __init__(self, latent_dim: int, hidden_dim: int, out_dim: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ELU(),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden_dim),
            nn.Dropout(0.2),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ELU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, out_dim),
        )

    def forward(self, z):
        return self.net(z)
```

### Full GVAE

`AnomalyGNN` wires the encoder and decoder together. The `reparameterize` method implements the reparameterization trick: during training, a random sample is drawn from the latent distribution using `z = mu + eps * exp(logstd)`. At inference, the mean `mu` is used directly.

```python theme={null}
class AnomalyGNN(nn.Module):
    """
    Graph Variational Autoencoder for node-level anomaly detection.

    Training objective: minimize reconstruction loss + KL divergence
                        + link prediction loss.
    Anomaly score     : per-node mean squared reconstruction error.
    """
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, latent_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = GNNEncoder(in_dim, hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        self.decoder = GNNDecoder(latent_dim, hidden_dim, in_dim)

    def reparameterize(self, mu, logstd):
        if self.training:
            std = logstd.exp()
            eps = torch.randn_like(std)
            return mu + eps * std
        return mu   # deterministic at inference time

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        mu, logstd = self.encoder(x, edge_index)
        z          = self.reparameterize(mu, logstd)
        x_recon    = self.decoder(z)
        return x_recon, mu, logstd, z

    def loss(self, x, x_recon, mu, logstd, edge_index):
        # Term 1: reconstruction accuracy
        recon_loss = F.mse_loss(x_recon, x, reduction="mean")

        # Term 2: KL divergence from standard normal prior
        kl_loss = -0.5 * torch.mean(
            1 + 2 * logstd - mu.pow(2) - (2 * logstd).exp()
        )

        # Term 3: link prediction (should edges exist between these nodes?)
        neg_edge    = negative_sampling(edge_index, num_nodes=x.size(0))
        pos_score   = (mu[edge_index[0]] * mu[edge_index[1]]).sum(dim=1)
        neg_score   = (mu[neg_edge[0]]   * mu[neg_edge[1]]).sum(dim=1)
        link_labels = torch.cat([
            torch.ones(pos_score.size(0)),
            torch.zeros(neg_score.size(0))
        ]).to(DEVICE)
        link_scores = torch.cat([pos_score, neg_score])
        link_loss   = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(link_scores, link_labels)

        total_loss = recon_loss + 0.5 * kl_loss + 0.3 * link_loss
        return total_loss, recon_loss
```

The three loss terms serve different purposes. Reconstruction loss teaches the model to accurately reproduce node features. KL divergence regularizes the latent space to prevent posterior collapse. Link prediction loss anchors the embeddings to the graph structure: similar nodes in the graph should be similar in embedding space.

### Instantiate Model and Optimizer

```python theme={null}
in_dim    = feat_tensor.shape[1]   # 11 features
model     = AnomalyGNN(in_dim, HIDDEN_DIM, LATENT_DIM).to(DEVICE)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(),
                             lr=LEARNING_RATE, weight_decay=1e-5)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=EPOCHS)

n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model ready | Parameters: {n_params:,}")
print(f"Architecture: {in_dim}d input -> {HIDDEN_DIM}d hidden -> {LATENT_DIM}d latent")
```

```text theme={null}
Model ready | Parameters: 16,459
Architecture: 11d input -> 64d hidden -> 32d latent
```

<Info>
  Weight decay of `1e-5` is mild L2 regularization. It is not strictly necessary for a model this size but helps prevent overfitting when the number of nodes (stocks) is small relative to the number of parameters.
</Info>

## What We Have So Far

At the end of Part 1, the following objects exist in memory and will be used in Part 2:

| Variable      | Contents                                                     |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `price_df`    | Wide DataFrame of daily close prices                         |
| `volume_df`   | Wide DataFrame of daily volume                               |
| `feat_df`     | 11-feature matrix, one row per stock                         |
| `feat_tensor` | Standardized features as a PyTorch tensor                    |
| `graph_data`  | PyTorch Geometric `Data` object with node features and edges |
| `nx_graph`    | NetworkX graph for visualization                             |
| `corr_matrix` | Full return correlation matrix                               |
| `model`       | `AnomalyGNN` instance, not yet trained                       |
| `optimizer`   | Adam optimizer                                               |
| `scheduler`   | Cosine annealing LR scheduler                                |

Continue to [Part 2](/recipes/gnn-anomaly-detection/gnn-part-2.mdx) to train the model, compute anomaly scores, and visualize the results.


# Part 2: Training, Scoring, and Clustering
Source: https://docs.sectors.app/recipes/gnn-anomaly-detection/02-gnn-part-2

By: [Alya Dwinanda](https://www.github.com/flytosevensky) · June 30, 2026

This is Part 2 of a three-part recipe. Part 1 covered data fetching, feature engineering, graph construction, and model definition. In this part, we train the GVAE, compute anomaly scores from reconstruction error, cluster the results, and produce a nine-panel visualization.

**Series overview:**

* **Part 1:** Setup, data fetching, feature engineering, graph construction, model definition
* **Part 2 (this article):** Training, anomaly scoring, clustering, visualization
* **Part 3:** Data quality audit, broker flow confirmation, foreign flow analysis, combined risk scoring

## Cell 6: Training Loop

The training loop is straightforward. Each epoch runs a full forward pass, computes the combined loss, backpropagates, clips gradients, and steps the optimizer and scheduler. Progress is printed every 20 epochs.

```python theme={null}
def train_epoch(model, data, optimizer):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    x_recon, mu, logstd, z = model(data.x, data.edge_index)
    total_loss, recon_loss  = model.loss(
        data.x, x_recon, mu, logstd, data.edge_index
    )
    total_loss.backward()
    # Clip gradients to prevent instability
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    optimizer.step()
    return total_loss.item(), recon_loss.item()


print(f"Starting training for {EPOCHS} epochs...")
loss_history = []

for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
    total_loss, recon_loss = train_epoch(model, graph_data, optimizer)
    scheduler.step()
    loss_history.append({
        "epoch": epoch,
        "total": total_loss,
        "recon": recon_loss
    })

    if epoch % 20 == 0 or epoch == 1:
        print(f"  Epoch {epoch:4d}/{EPOCHS} | "
              f"Total: {total_loss:.4f} | "
              f"Recon: {recon_loss:.4f} | "
              f"LR: {scheduler.get_last_lr()[0]:.5f}")

loss_df = pd.DataFrame(loss_history)
print(f"\nTraining complete. Final total loss: {loss_df['total'].iloc[-1]:.4f}")
```

Expected results:

```text theme={null}
Starting training for 200 epochs...
  Epoch    1/200 | Total: 6.0272 | Recon: 1.0983 | LR: 0.00500
  Epoch   20/200 | Total: 0.9167 | Recon: 0.5542 | LR: 0.00488
  Epoch   40/200 | Total: 0.9994 | Recon: 0.4307 | LR: 0.00452
  Epoch   60/200 | Total: 0.8946 | Recon: 0.4142 | LR: 0.00397
  Epoch   80/200 | Total: 0.7425 | Recon: 0.3539 | LR: 0.00327
  Epoch  100/200 | Total: 0.6771 | Recon: 0.3080 | LR: 0.00250
  Epoch  120/200 | Total: 0.6116 | Recon: 0.3777 | LR: 0.00173
  Epoch  140/200 | Total: 0.5869 | Recon: 0.3301 | LR: 0.00103
  Epoch  160/200 | Total: 0.5777 | Recon: 0.3018 | LR: 0.00048
  Epoch  180/200 | Total: 0.5516 | Recon: 0.3288 | LR: 0.00012
  Epoch  200/200 | Total: 0.5897 | Recon: 0.3510 | LR: 0.00000

Training complete. Final total loss: 0.5897
```

A healthy training run looks like this: total loss starts around 3.0 and drops rapidly in the first 25 epochs, then continues to decrease more slowly and stabilizes below 0.7 by epoch 150. Reconstruction loss tracks below total loss because it does not include the KL and link terms.

If the loss oscillates without converging, reduce `LEARNING_RATE` from 0.005 to 0.001. If it collapses to near zero within 10 epochs (posterior collapse), increase the KL weight from 0.5 to 1.0 in the loss function.

<Info>
  Gradient clipping at 1.0 is important here. GCN layers can produce large gradient norms when node degrees vary significantly, which is common in a correlation graph where hub stocks like BMRI are connected to many others while smaller stocks may have only a few edges.
</Info>

## Cell 7: Anomaly Scoring

After training, the model is switched to evaluation mode. The full graph is passed through once to get reconstructed features and latent embeddings. Per-node reconstruction error is computed as the mean squared error across all 11 features.

```python theme={null}
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    x_recon, mu, logstd, z = model(graph_data.x, graph_data.edge_index)

# Reconstruction error per node, per feature dimension
recon_error    = F.mse_loss(x_recon, graph_data.x, reduction="none")

# Average across feature dimensions to get a scalar score per node
anomaly_scores = recon_error.mean(dim=1).cpu().numpy()   # shape: (n_stocks,)
embeddings     = z.cpu().numpy()                          # shape: (n_stocks, 32)

# Threshold at the 90th percentile
threshold  = np.percentile(anomaly_scores, ANOMALY_PERCENTILE)
is_anomaly = anomaly_scores > threshold

# Build result DataFrame
result_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "ticker":        active_tickers,
    "anomaly_score": anomaly_scores,
    "is_anomaly":    is_anomaly,
}, index=range(len(active_tickers)))

# Attach original features for later analysis
result_df = result_df.join(feat_df.reset_index(drop=True))

anomaly_tickers = result_df[result_df["is_anomaly"]]["ticker"].tolist()
normal_tickers  = result_df[~result_df["is_anomaly"]]["ticker"].tolist()

print(f"Anomaly score range: {anomaly_scores.min():.4f} to {anomaly_scores.max():.4f}")
print(f"Threshold (p{ANOMALY_PERCENTILE}): {threshold:.4f}")
print(f"\nAnomalies detected ({len(anomaly_tickers)}): {anomaly_tickers}")
```

```text theme={null}
Anomaly score range: 0.0176 to 0.9454
Threshold (p90): 0.5319

Anomalies detected (3): ['BBCA', 'PGAS', 'SMGR']
```

<Info>
  The 90th percentile threshold means roughly the top 3 stocks in a universe of 30 will be flagged. Adjust `ANOMALY_PERCENTILE` to change the sensitivity. Lower values (e.g. 85) flag more stocks; higher values (e.g. 95) flag fewer but only the most extreme cases.
</Info>

## Cell 8: Clustering in Embedding Space

Clustering is done in two passes with different goals.

**KMeans on all stocks** maps the overall market structure into four groups. Stocks in the same KMeans cluster share similar graph-contextual representations regardless of whether they are anomalous or not.

**DBSCAN on anomalous stocks only** asks a more specific question: among the stocks that are already flagged as anomalous, do any of them share a common pattern, or did each become anomalous for independent reasons?

```python theme={null}
# Reduce embedding dimensions for visualization and clustering
pca           = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=42)
embeddings_2d = pca.fit_transform(embeddings)
print(f"PCA variance explained: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.2%}")

# KMeans: structure of the full market
kmeans         = KMeans(n_clusters=N_CLUSTERS, random_state=42, n_init=10)
cluster_labels = kmeans.fit_predict(embeddings)

# DBSCAN: structure of anomalies only
anomaly_mask = is_anomaly
if anomaly_mask.sum() >= 3:
    dbscan                = DBSCAN(eps=0.8, min_samples=2, metric="euclidean")
    anomaly_embeddings    = embeddings[anomaly_mask]
    anomaly_cluster_labels = dbscan.fit_predict(anomaly_embeddings)
    n_anomaly_clusters    = len(set(anomaly_cluster_labels)) - (
        1 if -1 in anomaly_cluster_labels else 0
    )
    print(f"DBSCAN: {anomaly_mask.sum()} anomalies -> {n_anomaly_clusters} clusters")
else:
    anomaly_cluster_labels = np.zeros(anomaly_mask.sum(), dtype=int)
    n_anomaly_clusters     = 1

# Attach cluster labels to results
result_df["kmeans_cluster"] = cluster_labels
result_df.loc[result_df["is_anomaly"], "anomaly_cluster"] = (
    anomaly_cluster_labels.astype(int)
)

# Silhouette score for KMeans quality
if len(set(cluster_labels)) > 1:
    sil_score = silhouette_score(embeddings, cluster_labels)
    print(f"KMeans silhouette score: {sil_score:.4f}")

# Summary of anomalies per DBSCAN cluster
anom_df = result_df[result_df["is_anomaly"]][[
    "ticker", "anomaly_score", "anomaly_cluster",
    "n_extreme_days", "n_volume_spikes", "volatility", "skewness"
]].copy()
anom_df = anom_df.sort_values(
    ["anomaly_cluster", "anomaly_score"], ascending=[True, False]
)
print("\nAnomalies by DBSCAN cluster:")
print(anom_df.to_string(index=False))
```

Expected results:

```text theme={null}
PCA variance explained: 38.82%
DBSCAN: 3 anomalies -> 0 clusters
KMeans silhouette score: 0.2018

Anomalies by DBSCAN cluster:
ticker  anomaly_score  anomaly_cluster  n_extreme_days  n_volume_spikes  volatility  skewness
  PGAS       0.945383             -1.0             3.0              0.0    0.028255 -1.279496
  BBCA       0.561426             -1.0             1.0              2.0    0.030549  0.516965
  SMGR       0.551280             -1.0             1.0              2.0    0.030296  0.353080
```

When DBSCAN assigns all anomalies to cluster -1 (the noise cluster), that is not a failure. It means the anomalies are isolated from each other in embedding space and should be investigated separately. When anomalies cluster together, it suggests a shared mechanism worth investigating.

## Cell 9: Nine-Panel Visualization

The visualization is built as a 3x3 grid of subplots. Each panel shows a different view of the results.

```python theme={null}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(20, 18))
fig.suptitle(
    "GNN Anomaly Detection — IDX Stocks\nSectors Recipe",
    fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", y=0.98
)

anomaly_color = "#e74c3c"
normal_color  = "#3498db"

# Panel 1: Training loss curve
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 1)
ax1.plot(loss_df["epoch"], loss_df["total"],
         label="Total Loss", color="#e74c3c", lw=2)
ax1.plot(loss_df["epoch"], loss_df["recon"],
         label="Recon Loss", color="#3498db", lw=2, ls="--")
ax1.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax1.set_ylabel("Loss")
ax1.set_title("Training Loss Curve")
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Panel 2: Anomaly score distribution
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 2)
ax2.hist(anomaly_scores[~is_anomaly], bins=20, alpha=0.7,
         color=normal_color, label="Normal", edgecolor="white")
ax2.hist(anomaly_scores[is_anomaly],  bins=10, alpha=0.8,
         color=anomaly_color, label="Anomaly", edgecolor="white")
ax2.axvline(threshold, color="black", ls="--", lw=2,
            label=f"Threshold (p{ANOMALY_PERCENTILE})")
ax2.set_xlabel("Anomaly Score (Reconstruction Error)")
ax2.set_ylabel("Number of Stocks")
ax2.set_title("Anomaly Score Distribution")
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Panel 3: PCA embedding space
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 3)
ax3.scatter(embeddings_2d[~is_anomaly, 0], embeddings_2d[~is_anomaly, 1],
            c=normal_color, alpha=0.6, s=60, label="Normal", zorder=2)
ax3.scatter(embeddings_2d[is_anomaly, 0], embeddings_2d[is_anomaly, 1],
            c=anomaly_color, alpha=0.9, s=120, marker="*",
            label="Anomaly", zorder=3)
for i, ticker in enumerate(active_tickers):
    if is_anomaly[i]:
        ax3.annotate(ticker,
                     (embeddings_2d[i, 0], embeddings_2d[i, 1]),
                     fontsize=7, ha="left", color="#c0392b",
                     xytext=(3, 3), textcoords="offset points")
ax3.set_title("GNN Embedding Space (PCA 2D)")
ax3.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%})")
ax3.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.1%})")
ax3.legend()
ax3.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Panel 4: KMeans clustering
ax4 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 4)
for c in range(N_CLUSTERS):
    mask = cluster_labels == c
    ax4.scatter(embeddings_2d[mask, 0], embeddings_2d[mask, 1],
                alpha=0.7, s=70, label=f"Cluster {c}")
for i, ticker in enumerate(active_tickers):
    ax4.annotate(ticker,
                 (embeddings_2d[i, 0], embeddings_2d[i, 1]),
                 fontsize=6, alpha=0.6,
                 xytext=(2, 2), textcoords="offset points")
ax4.set_title(f"KMeans Clustering (k={N_CLUSTERS})")
ax4.set_xlabel("PC1")
ax4.set_ylabel("PC2")
ax4.legend(fontsize=8)
ax4.grid(alpha=0.3)

# Panel 5: Top 15 anomaly scores bar chart
ax5 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 5)
top_n      = result_df.nlargest(15, "anomaly_score")
colors_bar = [anomaly_color if a else normal_color for a in top_n["is_anomaly"]]
ax5.barh(top_n["ticker"], top_n["anomaly_score"],
         color=colors_bar, edgecolor="white")
ax5.axvline(threshold, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5, label="Threshold")
ax5.set_xlabel("Anomaly Score")
ax5.set_title("Top 15 Anomaly Scores")
ax5.legend()
ax5.invert_yaxis()
ax5.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="x")

# Panel 6: Return correlation heatmap (first 15 stocks)
ax6 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 6)
subset     = active_tickers[:15] if len(active_tickers) >= 15 else active_tickers
corr_sub   = corr_matrix.loc[subset, subset]
mask_upper = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_sub, dtype=bool))
sns.heatmap(corr_sub, mask=mask_upper, ax=ax6, cmap="RdYlGn",
            center=0, annot=False, linewidths=0.3,
            vmin=-1, vmax=1, cbar_kws={"shrink": 0.8})
ax6.set_title("Return Correlation Matrix")
ax6.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90, labelsize=7)
ax6.tick_params(axis="y", rotation=0, labelsize=7)

# Panel 7: Feature profile of anomalous stocks
ax7 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 7)
if len(anom_df) > 0:
    features_to_plot = ["n_extreme_days", "n_volume_spikes", "volatility"]
    anom_plot        = anom_df.set_index("ticker")[features_to_plot]
    anom_plot_norm   = (anom_plot - anom_plot.min()) / (
        anom_plot.max() - anom_plot.min() + 1e-8
    )
    anom_plot_norm.plot(kind="bar", ax=ax7,
                        colormap="Set2", edgecolor="white", width=0.75)
    ax7.set_title("Anomaly Feature Profile")
    ax7.set_xlabel("")
    ax7.set_ylabel("Normalized Value")
    ax7.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax7.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45, labelsize=7)
    ax7.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")

# Panel 8: Correlation graph network (top 20 nodes)
ax8            = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 8)
subgraph_nodes = list(range(min(20, len(active_tickers))))
sub_G          = nx_graph.subgraph(subgraph_nodes)
pos            = nx.spring_layout(sub_G, seed=42, k=1.5)
node_colors    = [anomaly_color if is_anomaly[n] else normal_color
                  for n in sub_G.nodes()]
node_sizes     = [300 + anomaly_scores[n] * 2000 for n in sub_G.nodes()]

nx.draw_networkx_nodes(sub_G, pos, ax=ax8,
                       node_color=node_colors,
                       node_size=node_sizes, alpha=0.85)
nx.draw_networkx_edges(sub_G, pos, ax=ax8,
                       alpha=0.2, width=0.8, edge_color="gray")
labels = {n: active_tickers[n] for n in sub_G.nodes()}
nx.draw_networkx_labels(sub_G, pos, labels, ax=ax8, font_size=6)
ax8.set_title("Correlation Graph (Top 20 Nodes)\n"
              "Red=Anomaly  Blue=Normal | Size proportional to score")
ax8.axis("off")

# Panel 9: DBSCAN anomaly clusters
ax9 = fig.add_subplot(3, 3, 9)
if is_anomaly.sum() >= 3:
    anom_2d           = embeddings_2d[is_anomaly]
    anom_tickers_list = [t for t, a in zip(active_tickers, is_anomaly) if a]
    unique_clusters   = sorted(set(anomaly_cluster_labels))
    cluster_colors    = plt.cm.Set1(np.linspace(0, 0.8, max(len(unique_clusters), 1)))

    for ci, c in enumerate(unique_clusters):
        mask_c = anomaly_cluster_labels == c
        label  = f"Cluster {c}" if c >= 0 else "Outlier"
        color  = cluster_colors[ci] if c >= 0 else "black"
        ax9.scatter(anom_2d[mask_c, 0], anom_2d[mask_c, 1],
                    c=[color], s=150, alpha=0.85,
                    marker="*" if c >= 0 else "x",
                    label=label, zorder=3)
        for j, (x, y) in enumerate(anom_2d[mask_c]):
            ticker_idx = [k for k, m in enumerate(mask_c) if m][j]
            ax9.annotate(anom_tickers_list[ticker_idx],
                         (x, y), fontsize=8, fontweight="bold",
                         color="#8e44ad",
                         xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points")

    ax9.set_title(f"DBSCAN Anomaly Clusters ({n_anomaly_clusters} found)")
    ax9.set_xlabel("PC1")
    ax9.set_ylabel("PC2")
    ax9.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax9.grid(alpha=0.3)
else:
    ax9.text(0.5, 0.5, "Not enough anomalies\nfor DBSCAN\n(need >= 3)",
             ha="center", va="center", transform=ax9.transAxes, fontsize=12)
    ax9.set_title("DBSCAN Anomaly Clusters")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("sectors_gnn_anomaly_results.png",
            dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
plt.show()
print("Visualization saved.")
```

## Reading the Results

### Training Loss Curve (Panel 1)

A loss that drops sharply in the first 25 epochs then plateaus indicates the model has learned the main structure of the data. Continued slow decline after that is fine. A flat curve from epoch 1 indicates the learning rate is too low.

### Anomaly Score Distribution (Panel 2)

The distribution should be right-skewed: most stocks cluster near zero with a long tail of higher scores. The vertical threshold line separates normal from anomalous. If the threshold sits in a gap between two distinct clusters in the distribution, that is a good sign. If it cuts through a dense cluster, consider adjusting `ANOMALY_PERCENTILE`.

### PCA Embedding Space (Panel 3)

Stocks that cluster tightly in this space share similar graph-contextual representations. Anomalies that appear isolated from the main cluster are stocks whose behavior the GNN found hardest to explain given their graph neighbors. Anomalies that appear close to each other despite being flagged independently may share a root cause.

### Correlation Graph (Panel 8)

Node size is proportional to anomaly score. A large node in the center of the graph (a hub with many edges) that is also anomalous is the most interesting case: the GNN had a lot of neighbor information to work with, yet still could not reconstruct the stock's behavior. BMRI appeared this way in the sample run.

### DBSCAN Clusters (Panel 9)

Points labeled as "Outlier" (cluster -1) are anomalies that are isolated from all other anomalies in embedding space. This means they became anomalous for different reasons. In the sample run, all three anomalies were labeled as outliers, suggesting three independent anomaly mechanisms rather than a single shared cause.

## What We Have After Part 2

The pipeline has now produced a ranked list of stocks by anomaly score, with embedding-based cluster assignments. The next step is to validate these scores against independent market signals.

Continue to [Part 3](/recipes/gnn-anomaly-detection/gnn-part-3.mdx) to run a data quality audit, fetch broker flow and foreign flow data from the Sectors API v2, and compute a combined risk score that integrates all three signals.


# Part 3: Confirmation with Broker and Foreign Flow
Source: https://docs.sectors.app/recipes/gnn-anomaly-detection/03-gnn-part-3

By: [Alya Dwinanda](https://www.github.com/flytosevensky) · June 30, 2026

This is Part 3 of a three-part recipe. Parts 1 and 2 built and trained the GVAE and produced anomaly scores. In this part, we validate those scores against two independent market signals from the Sectors API: broker flow and foreign flow. We then combine all three signals into a single adaptive risk score for each stock.

**Series overview:**

* **Part 1:** Setup, data fetching, feature engineering, graph construction, model definition
* **Part 2:** Training, anomaly scoring, clustering, visualization
* **Part 3 (this article):** Data quality audit, broker flow, foreign flow, combined risk scoring

## Why Confirmation Matters

A GNN reconstruction error is a statistical signal. It tells you that a stock's behavior was inconsistent with what the graph structure would predict. It does not tell you whether that inconsistency reflects a real market event or is a modeling artifact.

Broker flow and foreign flow are independent market signals grounded in actual transaction data. If a stock has a high GNN anomaly score *and* its top broker is net distributing *and* foreign investors are net selling, the convergence of three independent signals is much stronger evidence than any one signal alone.

## Cell 11: Data Quality Audit

Before fetching confirmation signals, audit the result DataFrame for data quality issues. The two most common problems are zero-feature nodes (stocks with no trading data in the analysis period) and identical anomaly scores (which indicate duplicated or corrupted rows).

```python theme={null}
print("=" * 65)
print("  CELL 11: DATA QUALITY AUDIT")
print("=" * 65)

numeric_feat_cols = [
    "mean_return", "volatility", "skewness", "kurtosis",
    "max_return_zscore", "n_extreme_days", "max_volume_zscore",
    "n_volume_spikes", "price_vs_sma20", "vol_regime_ratio", "sharpe_ratio"
]

# Detect stocks where every feature is exactly zero
zero_mask         = (result_df[numeric_feat_cols] == 0).all(axis=1)
zero_data_tickers = result_df[zero_mask]["ticker"].tolist()

print(f"\nStocks with all-zero features (suspended or no data):")
if zero_data_tickers:
    for t in zero_data_tickers:
        row = result_df[result_df["ticker"] == t].iloc[0]
        print(f"  {t} | anomaly_score: {row['anomaly_score']:.6f} | "
              f"kmeans_cluster: {int(row['kmeans_cluster'])}")
    print(f"\n  Likely cause: stock suspended on IDX during {START_DATE} to {END_DATE}")
else:
    print("  None found.")

# Detect duplicated anomaly scores
score_counts = result_df["anomaly_score"].value_counts()
duplicated   = score_counts[score_counts > 1]
if not duplicated.empty:
    print(f"\nDuplicated anomaly scores detected:")
    for score, count in duplicated.items():
        affected = result_df[result_df["anomaly_score"] == score]["ticker"].tolist()
        print(f"  Score {score:.6f} appears in: {affected}")

# Remove zero-data stocks from downstream analysis
result_df_clean    = result_df[~zero_mask].copy().reset_index(drop=True)
active_tickers_clean = result_df_clean["ticker"].tolist()
anomaly_tickers_clean = result_df_clean[
    result_df_clean["is_anomaly"]]["ticker"].tolist()

# Borderline stocks: score above 75th percentile but not flagged as anomaly
p75_clean   = result_df_clean["anomaly_score"].quantile(0.75)
borderline  = result_df_clean[
    (result_df_clean["anomaly_score"] > p75_clean) &
    (~result_df_clean["is_anomaly"])
].sort_values("anomaly_score", ascending=False)

print(f"\nClean dataset: {len(result_df_clean)} stocks "
      f"(removed: {zero_data_tickers})")
print(f"Anomalies: {anomaly_tickers_clean}")
print(f"\nBorderline (above p75={p75_clean:.4f}, not anomaly):")
print(borderline[["ticker", "anomaly_score", "volatility",
                   "kurtosis", "n_extreme_days"]].to_string(index=False))

# Stocks to include in broker and foreign flow analysis
TARGET_TICKERS_BROKER = anomaly_tickers_clean + borderline["ticker"].tolist()
print(f"\nBroker analysis targets: {TARGET_TICKERS_BROKER}")
```

Expected results:

```text theme={null}
=================================================================
  CELL 11: DATA QUALITY AUDIT

Stocks with all-zero features (suspended or no data):
  WIKA | anomaly_score: 0.017637 | kmeans_cluster: 3

ticker  anomaly_score  volatility  kurtosis  n_extreme_days
  BMRI       0.529723    0.027713  4.121694             3.0
  INCO       0.516578    0.060206  1.340078             1.0
  INDF       0.364597    0.018867  1.100802             2.0
  ANTM       0.214800    0.044306  1.790394             2.0

```

<Warning>
  WIKA and WSKT both returned all-zero feature vectors in the sample run. Their anomaly scores were identical at 0.022838 because the model processed them as identical nodes. Suspended stocks are not anomalies in the meaningful sense and should be removed before interpretation. A suspended stock that stays in the graph can distort clustering by pulling other nodes toward its zero embedding.
</Warning>

## Cell 12: Broker Flow Analysis

Broker flow data is fetched from the Sectors API v2 endpoint `/v2/broker-summary/{symbol}/top/`. This endpoint returns the top net buyers and top net sellers for a given stock over the analysis period, aggregated across all trading days.

### A Note on the Zero-Sum Trap

The most common mistake when working with this endpoint is to compute a net total by summing all buyer net values and adding them to all seller net values:

```python theme={null}
# WRONG: always produces a result near zero
total = sum(b["net_idr"] for b in buyers) + sum(s["net_idr"] for s in sellers)
```

Equity markets are zero-sum. For every buyer there is a seller. The top 10 buyers and top 10 sellers in any stock will roughly cancel each other out when summed. The result is always close to zero regardless of the actual market dynamics.

The correct approach is a **dominance score**: compare the single largest accumulator against the single largest distributor.

```python theme={null}
# CORRECT: dominance score
top_buy_net   = buyers[0].get("net_idr", 0)   # positive: net bought
top_sell_net  = sellers[0].get("net_idr", 0)  # negative: net sold (API returns negative)
net_dominance = top_buy_net + top_sell_net     # positive = accumulation dominant
```

A positive dominance score means the biggest buyer in the market is accumulating more than the biggest seller is distributing. A negative score means distribution is outpacing accumulation.

### Utility Functions

```python theme={null}
def format_idr(value) -> str:
    """Format IDR values adaptively: Tr / B / M to avoid rounding small values to zero."""
    try:
        if pd.isna(value):
            return "N/A"
    except Exception:
        pass
    sign    = "+" if value >= 0 else "-"
    abs_val = abs(value)
    if abs_val >= 1e12:  return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e12:.2f}Tr"
    elif abs_val >= 1e9: return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e9:.1f}B"
    elif abs_val >= 1e6: return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e6:.0f}M"
    else:                return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e6:.2f}M"


def fetch_broker_top(ticker: str, start: str, end: str,
                     n_brokers: int = 10) -> dict:
    """
    Fetch top buyers and sellers for one stock.

    Endpoint: GET /v2/broker-summary/{symbol}/top/
    No date range limit (unlike /broker-summary/ which caps at 14 days).
    Costs 2 API credits per call.
    """
    url    = f"https://api.sectors.app/v2/broker-summary/{ticker}/top/"
    params = {"start": start, "end": end, "n_brokers": n_brokers}
    resp   = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params)
    return resp.json() if resp.status_code == 200 else {}
```

### Fetch Broker Data for All Stocks

```python theme={null}
print(f"Fetching broker data for {len(active_tickers_clean)} stocks...")
print(f"Endpoint: /v2/broker-summary/{{symbol}}/top/")
print(f"Period: {START_DATE} to {END_DATE}\n")

broker_top_all  = {}
broker_agg_rows = []

for ticker in active_tickers_clean:
    try:
        data    = fetch_broker_top(ticker, START_DATE, END_DATE, n_brokers=10)
        buyers  = data.get("top_buyers",  [])
        sellers = data.get("top_sellers", [])

        if not data or (not buyers and not sellers):
            print(f"  {ticker}: no data")
            continue

        # Dominance score: top accumulator vs top distributor
        top_buy_net   = buyers[0].get("net_idr", 0)  if buyers  else 0
        top_sell_net  = sellers[0].get("net_idr", 0) if sellers else 0
        net_dominance = top_buy_net + top_sell_net

        top_acc  = buyers[0]["broker_code"]  if buyers  else "n/a"
        top_dist = sellers[0]["broker_code"] if sellers else "n/a"

        broker_top_all[ticker] = data
        broker_agg_rows.append({
            "ticker":           ticker,
            "broker_net_total": net_dominance,
            "broker_buy_net":   top_buy_net,
            "broker_sell_net":  top_sell_net,
            "top_accumulator":  top_acc,
            "top_distributor":  top_dist,
            "n_buyers":         len(buyers),
            "n_sellers":        len(sellers),
        })

        flag = "RED" if ticker in anomaly_tickers_clean else "   "
        print(f"  [{flag}] {ticker:<6} | "
              f"Dominance: {format_idr(net_dominance):>14} | "
              f"Top acc {top_acc}: {format_idr(top_buy_net):>12} | "
              f"Top dist {top_dist}: {format_idr(top_sell_net):>12}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  {ticker}: ERROR {e}")

broker_result_all_df = pd.DataFrame(broker_agg_rows)
print(f"\nBroker data fetched: {len(broker_result_all_df)} / "
      f"{len(active_tickers_clean)} stocks")
```

<Info>
  The `/v2/broker-summary/{symbol}/top/` endpoint is preferred over `/v2/broker-summary/{symbol}/` for this use case because it has no date range limit and returns already-aggregated net values. The per-day endpoint caps at 14 days per request, requiring chunking for a 180-day window.
</Info>

### Patching broker data into confirm\_df

After fetching, use `.map()` instead of `.merge()` to assign broker values to the results DataFrame. This avoids column name conflicts when running cells iteratively.

```python theme={null}
# Build confirm_df from result_df_clean
confirm_df = result_df_clean[[
    "ticker", "anomaly_score", "is_anomaly",
    "volatility", "kurtosis", "skewness",
    "n_extreme_days", "sharpe_ratio", "kmeans_cluster"
]].copy()

# Map broker values directly to avoid merge conflicts
broker_map = broker_result_all_df.set_index("ticker")
confirm_df["broker_net_total"] = confirm_df["ticker"].map(broker_map["broker_net_total"])
confirm_df["broker_buy_net"]   = confirm_df["ticker"].map(broker_map["broker_buy_net"])
confirm_df["broker_sell_net"]  = confirm_df["ticker"].map(broker_map["broker_sell_net"])
confirm_df["top_accumulator"]  = confirm_df["ticker"].map(broker_map["top_accumulator"])
confirm_df["top_distributor"]  = confirm_df["ticker"].map(broker_map["top_distributor"])

print(f"Broker data mapped: "
      f"{confirm_df['broker_net_total'].notna().sum()} stocks")
```

## Cell 13: Foreign Flow Analysis

Foreign flow data is fetched from `/v2/foreign-flow/{symbol}/`. This endpoint returns daily net foreign inflow in IDR for one stock over a date range of up to 90 days.

The sign convention is straightforward: positive `net_foreign_inflow` means foreign brokers were net buyers on that day; negative means net sellers. Because the IDX is a closed market, domestic flow is always the exact negative of foreign flow:

```text theme={null}
domestic_net = -net_foreign_inflow
```

This means a single endpoint gives you both foreign and domestic sentiment.

```python theme={null}
def date_chunks(start_str: str, end_str: str, chunk_days: int = 90):
    """Split a date range into chunks of at most chunk_days days."""
    start  = datetime.strptime(start_str, "%Y-%m-%d")
    end    = datetime.strptime(end_str,   "%Y-%m-%d")
    chunks = []
    cur    = start
    while cur < end:
        chunk_end = min(cur + timedelta(days=chunk_days - 1), end)
        chunks.append((cur.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), chunk_end.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")))
        cur = chunk_end + timedelta(days=1)
    return chunks


def fetch_foreign_flow_v2(ticker: str, start: str, end: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Fetch daily net foreign inflow for one stock.

    Endpoint: GET /v2/foreign-flow/{symbol}/
    Max range: 90 days per request. Chunked automatically for longer periods.
    Response field: net_foreign_inflow (positive = foreign net buyers)
    Costs 1 API credit per call.
    """
    chunks   = date_chunks(start, end, chunk_days=90)
    all_rows = []

    for chunk_start, chunk_end in chunks:
        url    = f"https://api.sectors.app/v2/foreign-flow/{ticker}/"
        params = {"start": chunk_start, "end": chunk_end}
        resp   = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, params=params)

        if resp.status_code != 200:
            continue

        for point in resp.json().get("data", []):
            all_rows.append({
                "date":            point.get("date", ""),
                # Rename to foreign_net_buy for consistency with downstream code
                "foreign_net_buy": point.get("net_foreign_inflow", 0),
                "ticker":          ticker,
            })

    if not all_rows:
        return pd.DataFrame()

    df           = pd.DataFrame(all_rows)
    df["date"]   = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    return df.set_index("date").sort_index()


# Fetch foreign flow for all stocks
print(f"Fetching foreign flow for {len(active_tickers_clean)} stocks...")

foreign_data = {}
for ticker in active_tickers_clean:
    try:
        df_ff = fetch_foreign_flow_v2(ticker, START_DATE, END_DATE)
        if not df_ff.empty:
            foreign_data[ticker] = df_ff
            net = df_ff["foreign_net_buy"].sum()
            print(f"  {ticker}: {format_idr(net)} net over period "
                  f"({'inflow' if net > 0 else 'outflow'})")
        else:
            print(f"  {ticker}: no data")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  {ticker}: ERROR {e}")

# Aggregate foreign flow statistics
foreign_stats = []
for ticker in active_tickers_clean:
    if ticker not in foreign_data:
        continue
    ff   = foreign_data[ticker]["foreign_net_buy"]
    half = len(ff) // 2
    foreign_stats.append({
        "ticker":             ticker,
        "foreign_net_total":  ff.sum(),
        "foreign_avg_daily":  ff.mean(),
        "foreign_max_inflow": ff.max(),
        "foreign_max_outflow": ff.min(),
        "foreign_trend":      "improving" if ff.iloc[half:].mean() > ff.iloc[:half].mean()
                              else "worsening",
    })

foreign_result_all_df = pd.DataFrame(foreign_stats)
print(f"\nForeign flow available: "
      f"{len(foreign_result_all_df)} / {len(active_tickers_clean)} stocks")
```

### Visualizing Daily and Cumulative Foreign Flow

```python theme={null}
n_targets = len(TARGET_TICKERS_BROKER)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, n_targets, figsize=(6 * n_targets, 9))
if n_targets == 1:
    axes = axes.reshape(2, 1)

for col, ticker in enumerate(TARGET_TICKERS_BROKER):
    if ticker not in foreign_data:
        continue

    ff         = foreign_data[ticker]["foreign_net_buy"]
    cum        = ff.cumsum()
    is_anom    = ticker in anomaly_tickers_clean
    line_color = "#ef4444" if is_anom else "#f59e0b"

    # Top row: daily bar chart
    ax1        = axes[0][col]
    bar_colors = ["#22c55e" if v > 0 else "#ef4444" for v in ff]
    ax1.bar(ff.index, ff / 1e9, color=bar_colors, alpha=0.7, width=0.8)
    ax1.axhline(0, color="white", lw=0.8, ls="--", alpha=0.5)
    ax1.set_title(f"{'[ANOMALY]' if is_anom else '[WATCH]'} {ticker}\n"
                  f"Daily Foreign Flow",
                  color="white", fontsize=10)
    ax1.set_ylabel("Rp Billion", color="white")
    ax1.tick_params(colors="gray", labelsize=7)
    ax1.set_facecolor("#1e2330")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.15)

    # Bottom row: cumulative line chart
    ax2 = axes[1][col]
    ax2.plot(cum.index, cum / 1e9, color=line_color, lw=2.5)
    ax2.fill_between(cum.index, cum / 1e9, 0,
                     where=(cum >= 0), alpha=0.2, color="#22c55e")
    ax2.fill_between(cum.index, cum / 1e9, 0,
                     where=(cum < 0),  alpha=0.2, color="#ef4444")
    ax2.axhline(0, color="white", lw=0.8, ls="--", alpha=0.5)
    ax2.set_title("Cumulative Foreign Flow", color="white", fontsize=10)
    ax2.set_ylabel("Rp Billion (cumulative)", color="white")
    ax2.tick_params(colors="gray", labelsize=7)
    ax2.set_facecolor("#1e2330")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.15)

fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0f1117")
plt.suptitle("Foreign Flow — Anomaly and Borderline Stocks",
             fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="white", y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("sectors_foreign_flow.png",
            dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="#0f1117")
plt.show()
```

</Frame>

## Cell 14: Combined Risk Score

The final step merges GNN scores, broker dominance, and foreign flow into a single risk score per stock. Each signal is normalized to a 0 to 1 scale and combined with adaptive weights that depend on which signals are available for each stock.

### Normalization

```python theme={null}
def min_max_norm_safe(series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """
    Min-max normalize a series to [0, 1].
    NaN values are excluded from range computation but preserved in output.
    """
    valid = series.dropna()
    if len(valid) < 2 or valid.max() == valid.min():
        return pd.Series(0.5, index=series.index)
    return (series - valid.min()) / (valid.max() - valid.min())
```

### Mapping Foreign Flow into confirm\_df

```python theme={null}
ff_map = foreign_result_all_df.set_index("ticker")
confirm_df["foreign_net_total"] = confirm_df["ticker"].map(ff_map["foreign_net_total"])
confirm_df["foreign_avg_daily"] = confirm_df["ticker"].map(ff_map["foreign_avg_daily"])
confirm_df["foreign_trend"]     = confirm_df["ticker"].map(ff_map["foreign_trend"])

# Compute signals
# Note: signals are inverted for broker and foreign because outflow = higher risk
confirm_df["gnn_signal"]     = min_max_norm_safe(confirm_df["anomaly_score"])
confirm_df["broker_signal"]  = min_max_norm_safe(-confirm_df["broker_net_total"])
confirm_df["foreign_signal"] = min_max_norm_safe(-confirm_df["foreign_net_total"])
```

### Adaptive Weighting

The weight scheme adapts to available data rather than assigning zeros to missing signals.

```python theme={null}
print("=" * 65)
print(" CONFIRMATION DASHBOARD")
print("=" * 65)


def format_idr(value) -> str:
    """Format IDR values: Tr / B / M."""
    try:
        if pd.isna(value):
            return "N/A"
    except Exception:
        pass

    sign = "+" if value >= 0 else "-"
    abs_val = abs(value)

    if abs_val >= 1e12:
        return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e12:.2f}Tr"
    elif abs_val >= 1e9:
        return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e9:.1f}B"
    elif abs_val >= 1e6:
        return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e6:.0f}M"
    else:
        return f"Rp {sign}{abs_val/1e6:.2f}M"


# Ensure confirm_df already contains broker data from Cell 12.
# Only append foreign flow for tickers that are still missing.

assert "confirm_df" in dir(), "❌ Please run Cell 12 Final first!"
assert "broker_net_total" in confirm_df.columns, \
    "❌ confirm_df does not contain broker data — please run Cell 12 Final first!"

n_broker_ok = confirm_df["broker_net_total"].notna().sum()

print(
    f"\n✅ confirm_df loaded from Cell 12 Final: {len(confirm_df)} tickers, "
    f"{n_broker_ok} with broker data"
)
print(
    f"   Broker sample:\n"
    f"{confirm_df[['ticker','broker_net_total']].head(6).to_string(index=False)}"
)


# Fetch & merge foreign flow for all tickers
print(f"\n📥 Fetching foreign flow for all {len(active_tickers_clean)} tickers...")

foreign_data_all = {}

if "foreign_data" in dir():
    foreign_data_all = dict(foreign_data)

missing_ff = [
    t for t in active_tickers_clean
    if t not in foreign_data_all
]

print(f"   Already available: {len(foreign_data_all)} | Need to fetch: {len(missing_ff)}")

for ticker in missing_ff:
    try:
        df_ff = fetch_foreign_flow_v2(ticker, START_DATE, END_DATE)

        if not df_ff.empty:
            foreign_data_all[ticker] = df_ff
            net = df_ff["foreign_net_buy"].sum()
            print(f"   ✅ {ticker}: {format_idr(net)}")
        else:
            print(f"   ⚠️ {ticker}: empty")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"   ❌ {ticker}: {e}")


# Create foreign_result_all_df
foreign_stats_all = []

for ticker in active_tickers_clean:

    if ticker not in foreign_data_all:
        continue

    ff = foreign_data_all[ticker]["foreign_net_buy"]
    half = len(ff) // 2

    foreign_stats_all.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "foreign_net_total": ff.sum(),
        "foreign_avg_daily": ff.mean(),
        "foreign_trend":
            "up"
            if ff.iloc[half:].mean() > ff.iloc[:half].mean()
            else "down",
    })

foreign_result_all_df = pd.DataFrame(foreign_stats_all)

print(
    f"\n✅ Foreign flow: "
    f"{len(foreign_result_all_df)} / {len(active_tickers_clean)} tickers"
)


# Merge foreign flow into confirm_df
ff_cols = [
    "foreign_net_total",
    "foreign_avg_daily",
    "foreign_trend",
    "foreign_signal",
]

confirm_df.drop(
    columns=[c for c in ff_cols if c in confirm_df.columns],
    inplace=True,
)

confirm_df = confirm_df.merge(
    foreign_result_all_df[
        [
            "ticker",
            "foreign_net_total",
            "foreign_avg_daily",
            "foreign_trend",
        ]
    ],
    on="ticker",
    how="left",
)

print(
    f"   Foreign data merged: "
    f"{confirm_df['foreign_net_total'].notna().sum()} tickers"
)


# Calculate signal scores and combined risk score
def min_max_norm_safe(series: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:

    valid = series.dropna()

    if len(valid) < 2 or valid.max() == valid.min():
        return pd.Series(0.5, index=series.index)

    return (series - valid.min()) / (valid.max() - valid.min())


# Remove old signals before recalculation
signal_cols = [
    "gnn_signal",
    "broker_signal",
    "foreign_signal",
    "combined_risk_score",
    "risk_tier",
    "data_sources",
]

confirm_df.drop(
    columns=[c for c in signal_cols if c in confirm_df.columns],
    inplace=True,
)

confirm_df["gnn_signal"] = min_max_norm_safe(confirm_df["anomaly_score"])
confirm_df["broker_signal"] = min_max_norm_safe(-confirm_df["broker_net_total"])
confirm_df["foreign_signal"] = min_max_norm_safe(-confirm_df["foreign_net_total"])


def compute_combined(row):

    g = row["gnn_signal"]
    b = row.get("broker_signal", np.nan)
    f = row.get("foreign_signal", np.nan)

    hb = pd.notna(b)
    hf = pd.notna(f)

    if hb and hf:
        return g * 0.50 + b * 0.25 + f * 0.25
    elif hb:
        return g * 0.60 + b * 0.40
    elif hf:
        return g * 0.60 + f * 0.40
    else:
        return g


def risk_tier(score):

    if pd.isna(score):
        return "❓ NO DATA"
    elif score >= 0.65:
        return "🔴 HIGH RISK"
    elif score >= 0.40:
        return "🟡 MEDIUM RISK"
    elif score >= 0.20:
        return "🟠 WATCH"
    else:
        return "🟢 NORMAL"


confirm_df["combined_risk_score"] = confirm_df.apply(
    compute_combined,
    axis=1,
)

confirm_df["risk_tier"] = confirm_df["combined_risk_score"].apply(risk_tier)

confirm_df["data_sources"] = confirm_df.apply(
    lambda r: " + ".join(
        filter(
            None,
            [
                "GNN",
                "Broker" if pd.notna(r.get("broker_signal")) else "",
                "Foreign" if pd.notna(r.get("foreign_signal")) else "",
            ],
        )
    ),
    axis=1,
)

confirm_df = confirm_df.sort_values(
    "combined_risk_score",
    ascending=False,
)


# Print final table
print(
    f"\n{'Ticker':<7} {'GNN':>7} {'Broker':>16} "
    f"{'Foreign':>16} {'Combined':>9} Risk"
)

print("─" * 80)

for _, row in confirm_df.iterrows():

    b = format_idr(row.get("broker_net_total"))
    f = format_idr(row.get("foreign_net_total"))

    flag = "🔴" if row["is_anomaly"] else "  "

    print(
        f"{flag}{row['ticker']:<5} "
        f"{row['anomaly_score']:>7.4f} "
        f"{b:>16} "
        f"{f:>16} "
        f"{row['combined_risk_score']:>9.4f} "
        f"{row['risk_tier']}"
    )


# Dashboard visualization

tier_colors = {
    "HIGH RISK": "#ef4444",
    "MEDIUM RISK": "#f59e0b",
    "WATCH": "#f97316",
    "NORMAL": "#3b82f6",
    "NO DATA": "#64748b",
}


def bar_color(t):
    for k, v in tier_colors.items():
        if k in t:
            return v
    return "#64748b"


fig = plt.figure(figsize=(20, 13))
fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0f1117")


# Plot 1: Combined Risk Score
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, (1, 2))

ax1.barh(
    confirm_df["ticker"],
    confirm_df["combined_risk_score"],
    color=[bar_color(t) for t in confirm_df["risk_tier"]],
    edgecolor="none",
    height=0.7,
)

for thresh, color, label in [
    (0.65, "#ef4444", "High (0.65)"),
    (0.40, "#f59e0b", "Medium (0.40)"),
    (0.20, "#f97316", "Watch (0.20)"),
]:
    ax1.axvline(
        thresh,
        color=color,
        ls="--",
        lw=1.2,
        alpha=0.7,
        label=label,
    )

ax1.set_title(
    "Combined Risk Score — All Tickers\n"
    "(GNN 50% + Broker 25% + Foreign 25%)",
    color="white",
    fontsize=11,
)

ax1.set_xlabel("Score", color="white")
ax1.invert_yaxis()
ax1.set_facecolor("#1e2330")
ax1.tick_params(colors="white", labelsize=8)
ax1.legend(fontsize=8, facecolor="#2d3748", labelcolor="white")
ax1.grid(alpha=0.15, axis="x")
ax1.spines[["top", "right", "left", "bottom"]].set_visible(False)


# Plot 2: Signal Heatmap

heat_data = confirm_df.set_index("ticker")[
    ["gnn_signal", "broker_signal", "foreign_signal"]
].copy()

heat_data.columns = ["GNN", "Broker", "Foreign"]

ax2.set_title(
    "Signal Heatmap\n"
    "(red = high risk, gray = no data)",
    color="white",
    fontsize=10,
)

# Plot 3 title
ax3.set_title(
    "GNN Score vs Foreign Flow",
    color="white",
    fontsize=10,
)

ax3.set_ylabel(
    "Net Foreign Flow (Rp Billion)",
    color="white",
)

# Plot 4 title
ax4.set_title(
    "Broker Dominance Score\n"
    "(green = accumulation, red = distribution)",
    color="white",
    fontsize=10,
)

ax4.set_xlabel(
    "Net IDR (Rp Billion)",
    color="white",
)

# Plot 5 Summary

summary = "📋 FINAL SUMMARY\n"
summary += "─" * 30 + "\n\n"

summary += f"Total tickers : {len(confirm_df)}\n"
summary += f"Broker data  : {confirm_df['broker_signal'].notna().sum()} tickers\n"
summary += f"Foreign data : {confirm_df['foreign_signal'].notna().sum()} tickers\n\n"

summary += "🔴 HIGH RISK\n"

for _, r in high_risk.iterrows():
    summary += f"   • {r['ticker']} ({r['combined_risk_score']:.3f})\n"

summary += "\n🟡 MEDIUM RISK\n"

for _, r in medium_risk.iterrows():
    summary += f"   • {r['ticker']} ({r['combined_risk_score']:.3f})\n"

summary += "\n🟠 WATCH\n"

for _, r in watch_list.head(5).iterrows():
    summary += f"   • {r['ticker']} ({r['combined_risk_score']:.3f})\n"

if len(watch_list) > 5:
    summary += f"   ... +{len(watch_list)-5} more\n"

if "zero_data_tickers" in dir() and zero_data_tickers:
    summary += "\n⚠️ Excluded Data\n"

    for t in zero_data_tickers:
        summary += f"   • {t}\n"

plt.suptitle(
    "🎯 Confirmation Dashboard — GNN + Broker + Foreign Flow",
    fontsize=13,
    fontweight="bold",
    color="white",
    y=1.01,
)

plt.tight_layout()

plt.savefig(
    "sectors_confirmation_dashboard_final.png",
    dpi=150,
    bbox_inches="tight",
    facecolor="#0f1117",
)

plt.show()

confirm_df.to_csv(
    "sectors_confirmation_final.csv",
    index=False,
)

print("\n✅ Cell 14 (Final) completed!")

print("💾 Output files:")
print("   → sectors_confirmation_dashboard_final.png")
print("   → sectors_confirmation_final.csv")

print("\n🏆 Top 5 Combined Risk Scores:")

for _, r in confirm_df.head(5).iterrows():
    print(
        f"   {r['risk_tier']} {r['ticker']} | "
        f"Combined={r['combined_risk_score']:.3f} | "
        f"Broker={format_idr(r.get('broker_net_total'))} | "
        f"Foreign={format_idr(r.get('foreign_net_total'))}"
    )
```
